en: The Sūtra on the Buddha’s Former Birth as Siṃhacandra, newly translated with the translator’s name lost, appended to the Records of the Three Qin Dynasties.
Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying at the Kalandaka Bamboo Grove in Rājagṛha, together with...
He was accompanied by twelve hundred and fifty bhikṣus and one hundred bodhisattvas.

At that time, there was among the assembly a bodhisattva bhikṣu named Vasumitra, who was wandering through the Bamboo Grove, climbing up and down trees with a voice like that of a monkey, or grasping three bells to perform the *nārī* dance.
At that time, the local elders and passersby gathered in competition to watch him.
When the crowd had assembled, he rose into the air, leaped to the top of a tree, and made the sound of a monkey.
Eighty-four thousand golden monkeys gathered at Vulture Peak where the Bodhisattva was; the Bodhisattva further manifested various transformations to bring them joy.
At that time, the great assembly each spoke these words:
"The śramaṇa son of the Śākyas is like a child at play, deceiving and deluding the multitude. His evil deeds are not trusted by anyone; he even commits unrighteous acts with birds and beasts."
Thus, this evil reputation spread throughout the city of Rājagṛha.
A certain brahmin approached King Bimbisāra and addressed him, saying:
"Your Majesty, the śramaṇas, sons of the Śākya, are performing unlawful acts; they have even engaged in the Nara-dance with birds and beasts."
When the king heard these words, he resented the Śākyas and immediately commanded the elder Kalandaka, saying:
"These Śākyas have gathered many monkeys; what are they doing with them in your garden?"
“Does the Tathāgata know this?
The elder addressed the king:
“Vasumitra has performed a feat of transformation, causing all the monkeys to rejoice, while the devas have rained down flowers as an offering.”
"What has been done? This is something your servant does not know.
At that time, King Bimbisāra mounted a famous elephant and, escorted by attendants before and behind, proceeded to the place where the Buddha was.

Upon arriving at the Kalandaka Bamboo Grove, he immediately dismounted from his elephant. From afar, he saw the World-Honored One atop a multi-storied pavilion; his body was the color of purple gold, sixteen feet in height, seated upon a flower made of the seven treasures. The thirty-two marks and eighty minor characteristics all radiated light, like a mountain of purple gold situated amidst blazing flames, surrounded by a halo of golden light that caused the entire assembly to appear the same color—gold—including the Venerable Vasumitra and the eighty-four thousand monkeys, who were likewise turned to gold.

At that time, when the monkeys saw the Great King approaching, some sang, some danced, some beat drums, and some blew conch shells, performing various antics; among them were those who gathered flowers to present to the King.

Having seen this, the Great King, together with the great assembly, went to where the Buddha was. He paid homage to the Buddha, circumambulated him three times to the right, withdrew to sit on one side, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!
What merit did these monkeys possess in their past lives such that their bodies are golden?
And what transgression did they commit to be born among the animals?
Furthermore, Venerable Vasumitra, what merit did you plant in your past lives to be born into the family of a householder, and with faith in the homeless life, to leave the home and study the Path?

What further transgression have we committed that, though born among humans with all our faculties intact, we do not maintain the practice of the precepts, but instead associate with monkeys, our voices in song and speech being exactly like those of monkeys, causing the various non-Buddhists to mock us?
“I only pray that the World-Honored One will take pity on us and explain this in detail so that we may attain understanding!
The Buddha told the Great King:
“Listen attentively, listen attentively!
Reflect upon this well!
I shall analyze and explain it for you.
In the distant past, immeasurable billions of kalpas ago, before that time, there appeared in the world a Buddha named Dīpaṃkara, who was fully endowed with the ten titles.

After that Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, there were bhikṣus who practiced the Buddha-dharma in mountain marshes, fully observing the twelve dhūtas of an āraṇyaka and upholding the prohibitive precepts as a man protects his eyes. Because of this, they immediately attained the path of arhatship, possessing the three knowledges, the six supernormal powers, and the eight liberations.

At that time, there was a monkey in an empty marsh who went to where the arhat was; seeing the arhat sitting in meditative concentration, it immediately took the arhat’s sitting mat, draped it over itself as a *kāṣāya*, bared its right shoulder according to the manner of a śramaṇa, and walked around the bhikṣu holding an incense burner in its hand.
Then, that bhikṣu arose from his meditative concentration and, seeing that this monkey possessed a virtuous and wholesome mind, snapped his fingers and addressed the monkey, saying:
"O son of the Dharma!
"You should now resolve to attain the unsurpassed mind of enlightenment.

Upon hearing these words, the monkey leaped for joy; prostrating himself with his five limbs touching the ground, he paid homage to the bhikṣu, then rose and gathered flowers again to scatter over him.
At that time, the bhikṣu taught the three refuges to the monkey, saying:
"O son of the Dharma!
You should now follow and study the Buddha-dharma of the three periods of time; you ought to request and receive the three refuges and the five precepts."
At that time, the monkey immediately rose, joined his palms, and said:
"Virtuous One!
Please take note that I now wish to take refuge in the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha."
The bhikṣu says: "You should take refuge in the Buddha, take refuge in the Dharma, and take refuge in the Saṃgha.
He speaks thus a second and a third time.
"I have completed taking refuge in the Buddha, completed taking refuge in the Dharma, and completed taking refuge in the Sangha.
A second and third time, he should speak likewise:
"Next, one should perform repentance."
He addressed the monkey, saying:

"Throughout immeasurable kalpas of your previous lives, you were filled with greed, anger, ignorance, false views, envy, arrogance, slander, and the breaking of precepts; you committed all manner of evil deeds, fulfilling the ten non-virtuous actions. You committed the five heinous crimes, reviled the Vaipulya sutras, violated bhikṣuṇīs, and stole the property of the Saṃgha, committing countless and boundless grave offenses."
My present life is now exhausted; I shall not undergo further existence.
Great Arhat, you are able to eliminate the immeasurable heavy sins of sentient beings. Why is this so?

"When I was first born, I arose together with great compassion; such is the nature of the Dharma of the sages and saints of the three periods of time—they too arise in the world together with great compassion.
Thus, with earnest persistence, he three times spoke to the monkey regarding the confession for expiating transgressions.
Having finished the confession, he addressed the monkey, saying:
"Son of the Dharma!
Your present purity is called *poṣadha*. From this day forth until the end of your life, you shall receive the precept against killing."
"The Buddhas of the three periods of time and all Arhats have forever refrained from killing; their body, speech, and mind are pure, and you should be likewise.
At that time, the monkey said to the Arhat, "I vow to become a Buddha.
Following the words of the Venerable One, from this day until I attain Buddhahood, I shall never kill."
At that time, the Arhat heard the words of the monkey and, with body and mind filled with joy, immediately conferred upon him the five precepts:
"O son of the Dharma!
From this day forth until the end of your life, you shall study the Buddha-dharma accordingly."
The Buddhas of the three periods of time and their assemblies of śrāvakas have purified their physical karma; they never kill living beings and maintain the precept against killing.
Will you likewise, for as long as life lasts, maintain the precept against killing and be able to receive and uphold it?
The monkey replied, "I am able to uphold them.
He then received the precepts against stealing, sexual misconduct, false speech, and drinking intoxicants, all according to the aforementioned method.
Once he had received the precepts, the Arhat said to him: "You should make a vow.
You were a beast of burden; this present life obstructs the Path. Therefore, apply yourself with diligent vigor to seek Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi."
At that time, having finished making his vow, the monkey leaped up with great joy and ran toward a high mountain. He climbed a tree and danced about, then fell to the ground and died.
Because the Arhat had received the five precepts, he destroyed his karma for rebirth as an animal; at the end of his life, he was immediately reborn in the Tuṣita Heaven.

There he encountered a Bodhisattva in his last birth before Buddhahood, who explained to him the mind of the unsurpassed path. He then took celestial flowers and descended into an empty marsh to make offerings to the Arhat.
When the Arhat saw this, he immediately smiled and said:
"O Heavenly King!
The retribution for good and evil follows one like a shadow follows a form; they never depart from each other."
Then, the Arhat spoke in verse:
"Karma can adorn the body, following one from place to place;
Like a legal contract, it does not fail; Karma is like a man burdened with wealth."
That you are now born in the heavens is due to the karma of the five precepts;
that your previous body fell as a monkey was due to the nature of violating those precepts.
Upholding the precepts is the ladder for birth in heaven; breaking the precepts is the boiling cauldron.
I see those who uphold the precepts, their bodies adorned with radiant light.
They dwell in sublime pavilions made of the seven treasures, with the devas serving as their attendants.
Their beds and canopies are fashioned from various jewels, and they wear necklaces of mani-gems and flowers.
Encountering the Buddhas of the future, they joyfully discourse upon the sublime Dharma.
I see those who break the precepts falling into the hells,
where iron plows furrow their tongues and they lie upon beds of iron.
Molten copper flows from all four sides, burning and boiling their bodies;
some dwell upon mountains of knives, in forests of swords, or amidst boiling excrement;
in the hells of the Ash River and Cold Ice, they swallow iron balls and drink molten copper.
Such painful matters as these are constantly worn as ornaments for the body.
If one wishes to escape all hardships, avoid falling into the three evil realms,
travel upon the paths of gods and humans, and transcend to attain nirvana, [one must practice accordingly].
"One should diligently uphold the pure precepts, practice giving, and cultivate a pure livelihood.
When the Arhat had spoken this verse, he remained silent and without sound.
The Devaputra Monkey said:
"Venerable Sir!
What karmic offenses did I commit in my previous life to be born among the monkeys?"
"Furthermore, by what merit did you encounter a person of great virtue, escape birth as an animal,
and be reborn in the heavens? The Arhat replied,
"Listen attentively now!"
Reflect upon this well!
In the distant past, there appeared in this Jambudvīpa a Buddha in the world named Ratnamati Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, fully endowed with the ten titles, who manifested in the world.
After he had manifested the three kinds of parinirvāṇa, during the period of the Semblance Dharma, there was a bhikṣu named Padmagarbha who was a close friend to many kings, elders, and householders.

Those who live by wrong livelihood, are deceitful and crooked, and do not maintain the practice of the precepts, fall into the Avīci Great Hell at the dissolution of the body after death because of their delusive deception;
as swiftly as a strong man might extend or contract his arm, they are cast therein, their bodies filling the eighteen compartments like blooming lotuses.

Rain of hot iron balls enters through the crown of the head; hundreds of thousands of fierce fires and hot iron wheels descend from the sky, immeasurable and boundless; the lifespan in the Avīci Hell is one kalpa, and when the kalpa ends, one is reborn once more.

Having thus passed through the various great hells for a full eighty-four thousand kalpas, they emerge from the hells and fall among the hungry ghosts, where they swallow and drink molten copper and devour hot iron balls.
After eighty-four thousand years, he emerged from the realm of hungry ghosts; for five hundred lifetimes he was constantly born as an ox.
Furthermore, for five hundred lifetimes he was born among camels, for five hundred lifetimes among pigs, for five hundred lifetimes among dogs, and for five hundred lifetimes among monkeys.

"Because of his previous offering to a bhikṣu who maintained the precepts, and because of the solemn vow he made, he has now encountered me again; having bathed in my pure transformation, he has been reborn in the heavens.
The bhikṣu who maintained the precepts was none other than myself; the bhikṣu who was negligent was you."
At that time, having heard these words, the monkey-deva was struck with alarm and his hair stood on end; he repented of his former transgressions and immediately returned to the heavens.
The Buddha said to the Great King:

"That monkey, though an animal, upon seeing an arhat, received and upheld the Three Refuges and the Five Precepts. By virtue of this merit, he transcended the extremely heavy evil karma of a thousand kalpas and attained birth in the heavens."

Having encountered a Bodhisattva in his last birth before Buddhahood, from that time forward he encountered countless Buddhas, purely cultivated the Brahma-faring, fulfilled the six pāramitās, dwelt in the Śūraṅgama Samādhi, and abode on the stage of non-retrogression.
In his final body, following after Maitreya, he shall attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*; his kingdom shall be named Ratnaprabhāsa, and its land shall be as pure as the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven.
All sentient beings born in that land practice the ten wholesome deeds and possess the precepts without deficiency.

The Buddha’s name is Siṃhacandra Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Vidhyācaraṇasaṃpanna, Sugata, Lokavid, Anuttara, Puruṣadamyasārathi, Śāstā devamanuṣyāṇām, Buddha, Bhagavān. If there are sentient beings who hear the name of that Buddha, in every place where they are born, they shall always be far removed from the bodies of animals and eliminate the sins of birth and death for immeasurable kalpas.
The Buddha told the Great King:
"If you wish to know who that Lion-Moon Buddha of that land was, it is this very Bhikṣu Vasumitra in this assembly."

At that time, having heard these words, King Bimbisāra immediately rose and joined his palms; sweat flowed from his entire body, and he wept with tears raining down. Repenting and reproaching himself, he prostrated himself on the ground before Vāsulimitra, touching his head to the monk’s feet in salutation, and confessed his former transgressions.

The Buddha told the Great King: "If you wish to know who these eighty-four thousand golden monkeys are, they were, in the past during the time of Kāśyapa Buddha, eighty-four thousand bhikṣuṇīs from the two countries of Vārāṇasī and Kauśāmbī. They practiced various unrighteous acts, communicating with laypeople through messengers and violating the heavy prohibitions. They adorned their bodies like gandharva women, lacking any sense of shame; they made lust their necklace and their various transgressions of the precepts their flower garlands. They raised the banner of arrogance, beat the drum of conceit, plucked the lute of heedlessness, and sang songs of evil reputation. Mad, foolish, and ignorant like deluded monkeys, when they saw virtuous bhikṣus of good character and noble virtue, they regarded them as thieves."

"At that time, there was a bhikṣuṇī in that world named Śānti, who had attained arhatship, possessed the three knowledges and the six supernormal powers, and was endowed with the eight liberations. She went to where the bhikṣuṇīs were and said to them: 'Sisters!'"
While the World-Honored One was in the world, he often recited this verse:
"If there be a bhikṣuṇī who does not practice the eight respects, she is no daughter of the Śākya clan; she is like a caṇḍāla."
If there is a bhikṣuṇī who, through negligence, commits one of the eight grave offenses,
you should know that she is a great thief among gods and humans;
she shall dwell eternally in the Avīci Hell, passing through its eighteen layers.
The other three evil realms serve as their own gardens and groves;
for hundreds of thousands of immeasurable kalpas, they do not hear the names of the Triple Gem.
They also devour glowing iron balls and embrace copper pillars amidst the freezing ice.
When such karma has been exhausted, one will be born in the bodies of doves and pigeons,
venomous snakes and mongooses, centipedes and many-legged insects;
one must undergo all such various forms of existence.
When the bhikṣuṇīs heard this verse spoken by the arhat bhikṣuṇī, they harbored resentment in their hearts and reviled her with foul language, saying:
"Where has this old monkey come from?"
"Speaking evil words and false speech, you recklessly discourse upon the hells.
At that time, seeing those wicked people giving rise to unwholesome thoughts, the Arhat immediately conceived compassion and ascended into the void, performing the eighteen transformations.
When those wicked people saw the transformation, each removed their golden rings and scattered them over the Arhatī, saying:
"May our bodies be golden in color in every birth; we now repent for all the evil deeds we have previously committed."
‘We only pray that you will show us compassion and pity, and accept our offerings.
Then, that arhat bhikṣuṇī descended from the air and accepted the various offerings of those wicked women.

At that time, those evil persons, their bodies destroyed and their lives ended, fell into the Avīci Hell; like blooming lotuses, they filled the entirety of the hell and likewise passed through the other eighteen great hells in succession.
In each of those hells, their lifespan lasts for exactly one great kalpa; thus, they remain in the hells for a succession of ninety-two kalpas.
Upon emerging from the hells, they exist as hungry ghosts for five hundred lifetimes.
Emerging from the realm of hungry ghosts, they were constantly reborn as monkeys for a thousand lifetimes, their bodies golden in color.
Great King,
you should know that those eighty-four thousand bhikṣuṇīs who violated the precepts and reviled the arhats at that time are these eighty-four thousand golden monkeys present in this assembly today.
The one who at that time made offerings to those wicked bhikṣuṇīs is now this Great King.
Because of their past habitual tendencies, these monkeys have brought flowers and incense to make offerings to the Great King.
"The one who at that time defiled the precepts of that bhikṣuṇī is none other than Ghoṭamukha and the five hundred eunuchs of the king.
The Buddha told the Great King:
"One must be careful regarding the actions of body, speech, and mind."
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke in verse:
"Precepts are the medicine of ambrosia; Those who take them do not age nor die.
The virtue of the precepts is worthy of reliance; Its karmic reward always follows one."
By upholding the precepts, one attains peace and security; in whatever place one is born, there will be no suffering or calamity.
One shall also behold the Buddhas and, receiving the Dharma, attain liberation.
To break the precepts is to fall into hell, just like this monkey.
One’s place of birth will always be lowly and base, and the sufferings of hell will cut one to the core.
Great King, listen attentively!
Cease evil and cultivate all that is wholesome.
At that time, King Bimbisāra, having heard these verses, confessed before the Buddha; filled with shame and self-reproach, his mind was suddenly liberated, and he attained the stage of Anāgāmin.
The eight thousand followers whom the king had brought with him requested the king’s permission to go forth [into homelessness],
and the king immediately granted it. The Buddha said, "Welcome, bhikṣus!"

His hair and beard fell away naturally, the *kāṣāya* robe clad his body, and he immediately became a śramaṇa. He prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and before his head had even risen, he attained arhatship, possessing the three knowledges (*traividya*), the six superknowledges (*ṣaḍabhijñā*), and the eight liberations (*aṣṭavimokṣa*).
The remaining ten thousand six thousand followers whom the king had brought along all resolved to attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, and eighty thousand devas likewise resolved their minds upon it.

The eighty-four thousand golden monkeys, having heard this account of their past causes and conditions, felt shame and reproached themselves. They circumambulated the Buddha a thousand times and offered repentance before him; each of them also gave rise to the unsurpassed mind of bodhicitta. According to the length of their respective lifespans, they each passed away. After their deaths, they were reborn in the Tuṣita Heaven, where they encountered Maitreya and further advanced until they attained the stage of non-retrogression.
At that time, the Venerable Mahākāśyapa, having witnessed this event, addressed the great assembly:
"The conduct of a bodhisattva is so pure that it causes even animals to give rise to the aspiration for enlightenment."
"If even Vasumitra was able to perform such great Buddha-work, how much more so for other bodhisattvas whose majestic virtue is immeasurable?

At that time, the sons of the gods, the mountain deities, the earth deities, and the eight classes of beings—including devas and nāgas—seeing that the monkeys had resolved their minds on Bodhi and would be reborn in the heavens and attain non-retrogression, felt great joy in their hearts and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"After how long will these monkeys attain Buddhahood?"
The Buddha addressed the great assembly:

"After the passing of hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of nayutas of asankhyeyas of Ganges-sands of kalpas, there will be a kalpa named Great Radiance; within that kalpa, he shall attain Buddhahood."

Eighty-four thousand Buddhas appeared in succession within a single kalpa; they were all named Samantakāñcanaprabhāsarāja Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Vidhyācaraṇasaṃpanna, Sugata, Lokavid, Anuttara, Puruṣadamyasārathi, Śāstā devamanuṣyāṇām, Buddha, Bhagavān.

At that time, the great assembly, hearing the Buddha, the World-Honored One, bestow the prediction of Bodhi upon the monkeys, immediately removed the exquisite necklaces from their bodies to offer as worship to the Tathāgata and the community of bhikṣus. With one voice and in unison, they praised the immeasurable virtues of the World-Honored One, saying:
"The appearance of the Tathāgata in the world is precisely for the sake of these various monkey-like beings."
Excellent, World-Honored One!
If even a monkey who heard the Dharma can attain Buddhahood, how much more so will we ourselves not attain Buddhahood in a future age?
At that time, the great assembly, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, rejoiced and practiced accordingly; they paid their respects and withdrew.
Thus ends the *Sūtra on the Past Life of the Buddha Siṃhacandra*.
